doc.title: Tom Varner interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, August 13, 2025

title: Sisters' records and finding French horn jazz models
summary: His two older sisters' record collections; he played horn from fourth grade and discovered Julius Watkins, Jeff Stockham, John Clark, Amram, Willie Ruff, Graas.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Not – well my two sisters, I had two big sisters that loved music and loved – had these wonderful record collections from Judy Collins to The Beatles to Eric Dolphy, or the Pentangle, I used to joke about The Pentangle. Very sixties. So I had two big sisters, five years older and two years older, and that set some sparks I think, but they did not become professional musicians, but one is a very fine poet in Western Mass, she’s in the Greenfield, Massachusetts area. But from, so not music boundary pushers from my family, but I kind of just fell in love with – I played French horn since I was in the fourth grade. So by the time I was a high school junior I was like I really liked jazz more actually, now that I think about it but well I can’t really change instruments now, I’m too old. So I just stuck with it and then when I found out from a next door neighbor about Julius Watkins that helped me realize well then – Julius Watkins who actually went to high school I think with Sheila Jordan, or to the same high school, Cass Technic. But from age say 18 on I was getting that bug for thinking well maybe I could be a jazz improviser on this crazy instrument where now I found out that there were – I didn’t know about Jeff Stockham although he’s a little bit younger than me but not much. I then found out about John Clark and then I found about David Amram. Hopefully you could do a thousand interviews with them. Willie Ruff. I found out a little bit about John Graas – G-R-A-A-S, you probably know him. And then for a while there that was it. There were a few other, there were studio musicians who could really play in the jazz mode and/or

classical musicians who could play with a great jazz feeling, like Gunther Schuller or like Jimmy Buffington. But people who are real improvisers, there weren’t that many at the time when I was say 17 or 18. But it was slowly growing and it dawned on me that – and I was just a very stubborn kid. It was like this is what I want to do, and so I just kept at it.
